basis: Every tree here is derived from what a surface ARCHITECTURALLY is, not from a security assessment of any vendor. That a command-line agent running under your account can reach what your account can reach is a fact about command-line programs, true of all of them, and it is not a claim about whoever wrote one. Where a node comes from something stronger than that — a published third-party audit, or a direct measurement — the node says so and carries its date.

evidence.derived: Reasoned from what the surface is. True by construction, and nobody has checked this instance.
evidence.third-party: From a published read-only audit tool's module list, so the row is comparable with something public.
evidence.measured: Observed inside a running installation on the stated date. One vendor, one surface, one date. Not generalised.
evidence.tested: The boundary was probed by making requests rather than by reading documentation.

tiers.boundary: Enforced by something outside the grant — the OS, a separate account, a container, a network policy. It holds against a compromised agent.
tiers.setting: Enforced by the tool itself, running inside the grant. Anything that can run code here can go around it.
tiers.expectation: Enforced by nothing. Written in a prompt or a rules file. It is a mandate, not a control.
tiers.none: No mechanism is claimed. This is simply reachable.

surfaces.label: A command-line agent
surfaces.oneline: Runs under your user account, so it inherits your account's reach.

surfaces.label: A desktop application
surfaces.oneline: Also runs as you — the difference from a CLI is which prompts are on by default, and a default is a setting.

surfaces.label: A hosted assistant
surfaces.oneline: Reaches what you paste in and whatever connectors you switch on. Not your filesystem.

surfaces.label: A hosted agent container
surfaces.oneline: A container you do not control, holding the repository you attached to it.

facts.q: Are there credential files in your home directory?
facts.hint: Cloud config, kubeconfig, SSH keys, registry tokens — the usual dotfiles.

facts.q: Do any of them open a cloud or cluster account?
Do any of them push to a code host?
Do any of them publish packages or images?
Do you keep shell history or previous session transcripts?
facts.hint: A transcript is a superset of every file that session read.

facts.q: Can it run terminal commands for you?
facts.hint: Many desktop apps can, through a tool or an extension.

facts.q: Have you connected it to anything — mail, drive, a code host, an MCP server?
Do you paste or upload work files into it?
Does it have a repository attached?
Is a commit signing identity configured in it?

controls.label: It runs under a separate user account
controls.effort: hard — days, and it fights you
controls.note: The single largest reduction available, and the reason almost nobody does it is that it is genuinely difficult: paths, permissions, agents and editors all assume one account. Desktop applications frequently cannot be run this way at all.

controls.label: It runs in a container with only the project mounted
controls.note: Execution survives inside the container and stops being execution on your machine. The friction is real and recurring — mounts, tokens, editor integration.

controls.label: Outbound traffic goes through an allowlist
controls.effort: an hour, if you already have somewhere to put it
controls.note: The one control the hosted container already has, demonstrated rather than claimed. You can have it too.

controls.label: Credentials live somewhere the agent's account cannot open
controls.note: Only helps if the agent cannot become you — pair it with a separate account or a container, or it is a setting wearing a boundary's clothes.

controls.label: Permission prompts are on, with no skip flag set
controls.note: Worth doing and it is NOT a boundary: the prompt is enforced by the tool, and this grant can rewrite the file that disables it. Labelled honestly so you are not misled.

controls.label: No connectors are switched on
controls.note: The connector list is the whole of a hosted assistant's reach beyond the conversation. It is enforced by the vendor and it is genuinely outside the session.

controls.label: Only non-sensitive material goes in
controls.note: The hosted grant reaches what you put in front of it, and that part IS yours. It is an expectation rather than a boundary because nothing enforces it but you, every time.

cli.label: Runs as your user account
cli.detail: This is the grant. Everything below is a consequence of it rather than a separate decision — the agent inherits your account, so it inherits your account's reach.

cli.label: The conversation itself
cli.detail: Everything an agent does starts here, and it is the part nobody thinks of as a grant. It is drawn because a tool that only lists frightening capabilities is measuring its own framing rather than your setup.

cli.label: Read and write anything your account can
cli.detail: The folder restriction is enforced by the tool, which runs inside this grant. Anything that can execute as you can step around it — see the escalation edge from “Execute programs as you”.

cli.label: The project you are working on
Credential files in your home directory
cli.detail: A published read-only audit tool enumerates exactly this class: key files and their permissions, cloud and cluster credentials, registry tokens, code-host credentials. Nothing stands in the way, because the files are owned by the account the agent runs as.

cli.label: Shell history and past transcripts
cli.detail: A session transcript is a superset of every file that session read, so excluding a secret by path does not exclude its contents. Two independent routes reached this conclusion, which is why it is a finding rather than an observation.

cli.label: Its own configuration and rules files
cli.detail: A prompt that a flag in a writable file can disable is an expectation wearing a setting's clothes. The audit tool named below looks for exactly those flags in shell initialisation.

cli.label: Execute programs as you
cli.detail: This is the node that makes the two settings above cosmetic. It is why the escalation edges exist.

desktop.label: Runs as your user account
desktop.detail: A desktop application installed by you runs as you. The difference from the command line is which confirmations are on by default — and a default is a setting.

desktop.label: The conversation itself
desktop.detail: Everything an agent does starts here, and it is the part nobody thinks of as a grant. It is drawn because a tool that only lists frightening capabilities is measuring its own framing rather than your setup.

desktop.label: Read and write anything your account can
Credential files in your home directory
Its own settings and rules files

web.label: Runs in the vendor's environment
web.detail: This is the one place a hosted surface is structurally better: your filesystem is not reachable, and the boundary is enforced by something entirely outside the session. You also cannot inspect it, change it, or get it attested.

web.label: What you paste or upload
web.detail: This is the part of a hosted grant that is genuinely yours to control, and the only part. Everything you put in is inside the grant for as long as the conversation exists.

web.label: Connectors you switched on
web.detail: A connector moves a hosted assistant from “reaches what you paste” to “reaches an account”. It is enforced by the vendor and it is outside the session, so it is a real boundary — one you set, and one worth re-reading occasionally.

web.label: Your own machine's files
web.mechanism: the vendor's environment is not your machine

agentbox.label: Runs as root inside a vendor container
agentbox.detail: Measured inside one running session on 20 August 2026. Root inside the container, with passwordless escalation — so there is no internal boundary at all. One vendor, one surface, one date, and the vendor is not named because the point is the taxonomy rather than the grade.

agentbox.label: Your own machine's files
agentbox.mechanism: the container is not your machine

agentbox.label: Credential stores in the image
agentbox.mechanism: present, and empty of usable material

agentbox.label: Outbound network
agentbox.mechanism: an egress allowlist the process cannot edit
agentbox.detail: Probed by making two requests: a package index resolved, an arbitrary public host did not. It is a real boundary for a precise reason — the agent is root, and root cannot defeat it, because nothing inside the container enforces it. This is the only tier-one boundary in the whole library, and it is published because a page that only reports unfavourable findings is doing advocacy rather than measurement.

escalations.why: Anything that can run programs as you can rewrite the file that turns the prompt off.
The folder restriction is enforced by the tool. Execution as you goes around it.

capabilities.label: Draft or edit a document for me
Explain code or a file I show it
Read the project it is working on
Change the project it is working on
Reach a permitted list of hosts
Reach any host on the internet
Publish packages and images as you
Act in your cloud and cluster accounts
Read your shell history and past sessions

examples.label: A developer on a laptop
examples.blurb: One CLI agent, credentials in the home directory, no containment. The common case, and the one with the widest gap.

examples.label: The same developer, contained
examples.blurb: The same agent, in a container, with an egress allowlist. Shows what the controls actually remove.

examples.label: A team using three surfaces
examples.blurb: A CLI on the laptop, a hosted assistant in the browser, and a hosted agent container. Three shapes, one dashboard.

examples.label: No local agents at all
examples.blurb: Only a hosted assistant, no connectors. The smallest grant in the library — and the one you can least verify.

rerun.cli: Run a published read-only agent-risk audit against your own machine — e.g. github.com/bartek-filipiuk/ai-agent-audit — and compare its modules with the nodes here. It reports path, type, count and a redacted fingerprint, and never leaves your machine.
rerun.desktop: The same audit covers a desktop install: what matters is which account the application runs under, and whether it can run commands.
rerun.web: Open the connector or integration settings and list what is switched on. That list is the whole of the grant beyond the conversation.
rerun.agentbox: Inside a session, check the process identity, look for an attestation device, and probe egress by requesting one expected host and one arbitrary one. Two requests is the whole test.
